# Machine-Generated Files Under Version Control

Most ecosystems commit at least one file their own toolchain rewrites. A merge conflict in
those files is not a prose conflict, and the three-field diff tool you would reach for is the
wrong tool. This is about telling generated files from authored ones, and knowing which
regeneration command belongs to each.

## When to Use

- A merge or rebase stops with a conflict in `go.sum`, `uv.lock`, `packages.lock.json`,
  `gradle-wrapper.jar`, or a similar artifact.
- A review comment asks someone to "fix the conflict in the lock file" by hand.
- A lock file is being added to `.gitignore` to stop conflicts — check whether the ecosystem
  says to commit it first; two of the three below say to commit, and one says to commit it
  only for applications.
- A lock file is being committed, but nobody can say which command regenerates it or what
  CI does to verify it.

## Usage Example

### The rule

A generated file is never hand-merged. Take the whole file from one side, then regenerate
with the toolchain so the result is what the tool would have written anyway. The point of
regenerating rather than picking a side is that the tool resolves *both* branches' intent —
an additive edit in a lock file is real intent, and `--ours` silently drops it.

### The procedure

```bash
# Python — uv. From the uv maintainer, on the lockfile conflict:
git checkout <parent> -- uv.lock
uv lock

# Go — go.sum. The Go docs state that go mod tidy "will add missing hashes and will
# remove unnecessary hashes from go.sum", so the file is fully derived:
git checkout <parent> -- go.sum
go mod tidy

# .NET — packages.lock.json. Opt in first, then force re-resolution:
#   <RestorePackagesWithLockFile>true</RestorePackagesWithLockFile>
dotnet restore --force-evaluate

# Gradle — the wrapper JAR. Regenerated by the :wrapper task:
./gradlew :wrapper
```

Then commit the regenerated file on its own or with the change that caused it, and verify
the regeneration is what CI will do — a lock file that is correct on your machine and stale
in CI is a worse failure than the conflict was.

### What each toolchain actually commits

| Ecosystem | File | Committed? | Regenerate with | Hand-mergeable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Go | `go.mod` | yes | `go mod tidy`, `go mod edit` | yes — it is an authored, sorted manifest |
| Go | `go.sum` | yes | `go mod tidy` | no — derived hashes |
| Python | `uv.lock` | yes | `uv lock` | no — derived |
| .NET | `packages.lock.json` | **applications only** | `dotnet restore --force-evaluate` | no — derived closure |
| Gradle | `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar` | yes, and expected | `gradle :wrapper` | no — binary |
| Gradle | `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` | yes | `gradle :wrapper --gradle-version X` | yes — hand-editable |
| Gradle | `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat` | yes | `gradle :wrapper` | generated, but no conflict to resolve |

The Go row pair is the general case, and it is worth stating as a rule: **`go.mod` is
authored, `go.sum` is derived.** The Go Modules Reference describes `go.sum` as holding
"cryptographic hashes of the module's direct and indirect dependencies" that the go command
computes on download, and says plainly that `go mod tidy` adds missing hashes and removes
unnecessary ones. `go.mod` by contrast is a list of requirements you wrote; merging two
people's added requirements is ordinary text merging. Assuming the same rule for both, or
the reverse, produces either a corrupt hash file or a silently dropped dependency.

## Caveats

- **`gradle-wrapper.jar` is binary and there is no way around committing it.** Gradle's own
  words: *"Wrapper files, including the JAR file, are small. Adding the JAR file to version
  control is expected. Some organizations do not allow projects to submit binary files to
  version control, and there is no workaround available."* So a conflict there is resolved by
  regenerating with the target Gradle version, not by merging. There is also a documented
  verification path (checksum validation, PGP, and automatic verification on GitHub) — if
  your organisation forbids binaries, that is a policy conversation, not a git setting.
- **Do not commit `packages.lock.json` for library projects.** NuGet says to check it in for
  applications and executables, and *not* for libraries or shared common-code projects:
  *"the lock file of a common code project has little say over the packages resolved for
  projects that depend on it."* Committing it there looks harmless and does nothing.
- **Locked mode turns a stale lock file into a build failure, which is the point.** With
  `RestoreLockedMode`, restore either uses exactly the listed packages or fails. That is the
  mechanism that catches a lock file that was hand-edited into an inconsistent state.
- **A floating version in a project file makes the lock file change without your input.**
  NuGet documents that restore will not re-resolve on its own unless you pass
  `--force-evaluate`, which is what makes `4.*`-style references a recurring diff source.
- **The SDK version can silently change your lock file.** NuGet notes that the .NET SDK adds
  implicit `PackageReference` items, so a different SDK version changes package versions and
  causes locked-mode restore failures. Their recommended fix is a `global.json` with a
  `rollForward` policy. This is the same failure as a stale lock file but with a different
  cause — check the SDK before assuming someone edited the file.
- **Python lock files can be in a permanent conflict loop.** A project whose version comes
  from git tags (setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs) records that version in the lock file, so every
  commit makes the lock file stale and every automated version bump produces a conflict on a
  line nobody changed on purpose. uv now omits dynamic versions for editable packages, which
  removes most of it, but for older lock files the honest fix is to bump the version in the
  lock file deliberately (`uv lock --upgrade-package <name>`, or `uv version --bump`) rather
  than to resolve the conflict by picking a side.
- **This is not a general merge strategy.** It applies to files a toolchain derives. Your
  source files merge normally.
